response: Laminoplasty outcomes can differ between patients with degenerative stenosis and those with ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL). Generally, patients with degenerative stenosis tend to have better outcomes after laminoplasty, with improved neurological function and reduced symptoms. In contrast, patients with OPLL may have more variable outcomes, with some studies suggesting that they may be at higher risk for incomplete decompression, residual or recurrent symptoms, and poorer neurological recovery. This is because OPLL can be a more complex and challenging condition to treat, with a higher risk of dural adhesion and incomplete removal of the ossified ligament. However, overall, laminoplasty can still be an effective treatment option for both conditions, and individual outcomes depend on various factors, including the severity of the condition, surgical technique, and patient-specific characteristics.
